claims.claim_text: 37signals/Basecamp initiated a public cloud exit after a roughly $3.2M annual cloud baseline and claimed roughly $10M in five-year savings.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 1
claims.rationale: The official Basecamp cloud-exit portal is the right primary source, but basecamp.com is not on the current allowlist.

claims.claim_text: The 37signals cloud migration took eight months of engineering time.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 2
claims.rationale: The timing is part of the official 37signals/Basecamp cloud-exit timeline, but the primary source host is off-allowlist.

claims.claim_text: The module says 37signals replaced Amazon RDS with highly available self-managed PostgreSQL clusters.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 2
claims.anchor_text: Managed relational databases (Amazon RDS) were replaced by highly available, self-managed PostgreSQL clusters.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Managed relational databases had to be replaced with self-managed database infrastructure.
claims.rationale: Official 37signals material discusses managed database replacement, but the PostgreSQL-specific detail is not supported as written.

claims.claim_text: The module says 37signals replaced ElastiCache with manually operated Redis Sentinel deployments.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 2
claims.anchor_text: In-memory data stores (Amazon ElastiCache) were swapped for manually operated Redis Sentinel deployments.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Managed cache services had to be replaced with self-managed cache infrastructure.
claims.rationale: The operational lesson is valid, but the exact replacement architecture is an uncited company-specific detail.

claims.claim_text: The module says 37signals migrated ALB routing to HAProxy and NGINX instances.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 2
claims.anchor_text: Managed routing (Application Load Balancers) was migrated to HAProxy and NGINX instances.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Managed routing had to be replaced with self-managed routing and proxy infrastructure.
claims.rationale: The sentence gives specific replacement components for a named migration without a primary citation in the allowlist.

claims.claim_text: The module says 37signals replaced CloudWatch with full Prometheus and Grafana stacks.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 2
claims.anchor_text: Furthermore, proprietary observability (CloudWatch) had to be replaced with full Prometheus and Grafana stacks.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Furthermore, observability had to be rebuilt with self-managed tooling.
claims.rationale: 37signals has written about Prometheus, but the full CloudWatch-to-Prometheus-and-Grafana replacement claim is too specific without a direct source.

claims.claim_text: The module says 37signals completed the bulk of the migration by early 2023.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 3
claims.anchor_text: By early 2023, 37signals successfully completed the bulk of the migration, achieving the massive infrastructure cost reductions they hypothesized.
claims.suggested_rewrite: The 37signals story is most useful as an operational lesson: major cost reductions only matter if the organization can complete and operate the replacement platform.
claims.rationale: The exact completion timing is too brittle and appears inconsistent with the public migration timeline.

claims.claim_text: The module says 37signals had to hire additional specialized systems engineers.
claims.span_hint: section: Why This Module Matters | paragraph 3
claims.anchor_text: However, achieving this required them to hire additional specialized systems engineers and spend months stabilizing their new self-managed database infrastructure.
claims.suggested_rewrite: However, achieving this still required sustained operational discipline and careful stabilization of the new self-managed infrastructure.
claims.rationale: The official cloud-exit portal says the migration was done without adding staff, so the hiring claim should be removed.

claims.claim_text: The module calls its repatriation decision matrix an industry-standard matrix.
claims.span_hint: section: The Economics of Cloud Repatriation | before Mermaid diagram
claims.anchor_text: Here is the baseline, industry-standard decision matrix for evaluating a repatriation effort.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Here is a practical decision matrix for stress-testing a repatriation effort.
claims.rationale: No primary source establishes these thresholds as an industry standard.

claims.claim_text: The module presents a precise annual cloud-vs-on-prem financial table as a typical breakdown.
claims.span_hint: section: The Economics of Cloud Repatriation | before TCO table
claims.anchor_text: The financial breakdown typically looks like the following table when amortizing high-density datacenter hardware over a standard four-year lifecycle.
claims.suggested_rewrite: A simplified financial model might look like the following when amortizing high-density datacenter hardware over a multi-year lifecycle.
claims.rationale: The exact table values are pedagogical, so the prose should frame them as an illustrative model rather than a typical market benchmark.

claims.claim_text: The module states that cloud is almost always cheaper at 20 nodes and that repatriation breakeven is typically 50-100 nodes.
claims.span_hint: section: The Economics of Cloud Repatriation | Warning block
claims.anchor_text: At 20 nodes, cloud is almost always cheaper when you factor in staff time. Breakeven is typically 50-100 nodes depending on workload density and cloud discounts (Reserved Instances, Committed Use Discounts).
claims.suggested_rewrite: At smaller cluster sizes, staff time can erase hardware savings; breakeven depends on workload density, staffing model, negotiated discounts, and support requirements.
claims.rationale: The node-count thresholds are uncited and too workload-dependent to present as factual statistics.

claims.claim_text: AWS Outposts includes 42U rack and 1U/2U server form factors and AWS manages the Outposts hardware/service link model.
claims.span_hint: section: Hybrid Cloud and Partial Repatriation Alternatives | AWS Outposts bullet
claims.rationale: The AWS Outposts user guide documents 42U racks, 1U/2U servers, AWS-managed hardware, and the service link to an AWS Region.

claims.claim_text: The module says second-generation Outposts racks expanded to over 20 additional countries in January 2026.
claims.span_hint: section: Hybrid Cloud and Partial Repatriation Alternatives | AWS Outposts bullet
claims.anchor_text: Second-generation Outposts racks expanded to over 20 additional countries in January 2026.
claims.suggested_rewrite: AWS announced additional regional support for second-generation Outposts racks in January 2026.
claims.rationale: The AWS announcement supports additional regional support, not the specific over-20-countries claim as written.

claims.claim_text: Google Distributed Cloud provides managed software and hardware options for data centers and edge locations.
claims.span_hint: section: Hybrid Cloud and Partial Repatriation Alternatives | Google Distributed Cloud bullet
claims.rationale: The Google Distributed Cloud documentation describes connected, air-gapped, and software-only components for edge and data-center use.

claims.claim_text: The module states that Anthos has been officially retired across all Google documentation and partner programs.
claims.span_hint: section: Hybrid Cloud and Partial Repatriation Alternatives | Google Distributed Cloud bullet
claims.anchor_text: - **Google Distributed Cloud (GDC)**: Formerly known by the brand name Anthos (which has been officially retired across all Google documentation and partner programs), GDC provides comprehensive hardware and software solutions to execute Google Cloud services securely at the edge or deep within your private datacenter infrastructure.
claims.suggested_rewrite: - **Google Distributed Cloud (GDC)**: GDC provides hardware and software solutions to run Google Cloud services at the edge or within private datacenter infrastructure.
claims.rationale: Google documentation still contains Anthos references, so the blanket retirement claim is too broad.

claims.claim_text: Azure Arc projects on-premises and non-Azure servers, Kubernetes clusters, and data services into Azure Resource Manager for centralized management, policy, and monitoring.
claims.span_hint: section: Hybrid Cloud and Partial Repatriation Alternatives | Azure Arc bullet
claims.rationale: Microsoft's Azure Arc overview directly lists servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services, and SQL Server as supported resource types.

claims.claim_text: Azure Arc Gateway for Arc-enabled Kubernetes reached general availability in early 2026.
claims.span_hint: section: Hybrid Cloud and Partial Repatriation Alternatives | Azure Arc bullet
claims.rationale: The Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes release notes list the general availability of Azure Arc gateway for Kubernetes.

claims.claim_text: Crossplane is a CNCF Graduated project for building declarative cloud-native control planes.
claims.span_hint: section: Virtualization in the Container Era | Crossplane paragraph
claims.rationale: The CNCF project page lists Crossplane as Graduated and describes its control-plane role.

claims.claim_text: The module says Crossplane's current stable version is v2.2.0 released on February 17, 2025.
claims.span_hint: section: Virtualization in the Container Era | Crossplane paragraph
claims.anchor_text: with its current stable version v2.2.0 released on February 17, 2025
claims.suggested_rewrite: with current release details documented by the upstream project
claims.rationale: The date is stale/incorrect and 'current stable' claims change too quickly to hard-code in this module.

claims.claim_text: KubeVirt is a CNCF Incubating project and KubeVirt v1.8 was announced on March 25, 2026 aligned with Kubernetes v1.35.
claims.span_hint: section: Virtualization in the Container Era | KubeVirt paragraph
claims.rationale: The CNCF KubeVirt v1.8 announcement states the March 25, 2026 release and alignment with Kubernetes v1.35.

claims.claim_text: The module says KubeVirt is rapidly approaching CNCF graduation.
claims.span_hint: section: Virtualization in the Container Era | KubeVirt paragraph
claims.anchor_text: that is rapidly approaching graduation
claims.suggested_rewrite: with an active release cadence
claims.rationale: Graduation timing is a prediction and is not established by the CNCF project status.

claims.claim_text: Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization 4.21 is generally available and includes VM management capabilities integrated with OpenShift.
claims.span_hint: section: Virtualization in the Container Era | OpenShift Virtualization paragraph
claims.rationale: Red Hat's release post states that OpenShift Virtualization 4.21 is generally available and summarizes new VM management capabilities.

claims.claim_text: The module gives a current Harvester v1.7.1 release date and says Harvester has no CNCF maturity level.
claims.span_hint: section: Virtualization in the Container Era | Harvester note
claims.anchor_text: *An important distinction must be made regarding vendor claims in the virtualization space: Sources frequently conflate Harvester being 'built on CNCF projects' with it being a CNCF project itself. According to the official CNCF project landscape, SUSE/Rancher's Harvester HCI (current stable v1.7.1, released February 10, 2025) does not appear as a named project and does not have an official CNCF maturity level, despite utilizing CNCF projects like KubeVirt and Longhorn under the hood.*
claims.suggested_rewrite: *An important distinction must be made regarding vendor claims in the virtualization space: Harvester is a SUSE/Rancher HCI product built on Kubernetes and related cloud-native projects; verify its current release and CNCF status directly before treating it as a CNCF-hosted project.*
claims.rationale: The release date is stale/incorrect, and the CNCF-status claim should be verified live rather than embedded with a brittle version parenthetical.

claims.claim_text: AWS Load Balancer Controller Ingress annotations include ALB scheme, certificate, WAF, target type, health check, and SSL redirect settings.
claims.span_hint: section: AWS ALB Annotation Translation | translation table
claims.rationale: The AWS Load Balancer Controller annotation reference documents the ALB annotations named in the module.

claims.claim_text: The module says AWS ALB provisions a fleet of underlying EC2 instances and scales it based on ingress bandwidth.
claims.span_hint: section: Translating Cloud Networking to Bare Metal | paragraph 1
claims.anchor_text: AWS silently provisions a fleet of underlying EC2 instances, manages the high-availability failover, and scales the fleet up and down based on your ingress bandwidth.
claims.suggested_rewrite: AWS provisions and operates the managed load balancer infrastructure, including availability and capacity management behind the service.
claims.rationale: AWS documentation supports managed load balancer infrastructure, but not customer-visible underlying EC2 instances as written.

claims.claim_text: MetalLB BGP mode establishes BGP sessions from cluster nodes to routers and advertises external service IPs.
claims.span_hint: section: Translating Cloud Networking to Bare Metal | MetalLB paragraph
claims.rationale: The MetalLB BGP concept page is the primary source, but metallb.io is not on the allowlist.

claims.claim_text: A missing WAF annotation can remove an application firewall control during migration.
claims.span_hint: section: AWS ALB Annotation Translation | paragraph after table
claims.rationale: OWASP describes WAFs as application-layer controls that filter, monitor, and block HTTP traffic.

claims.claim_text: The module says transferring 50TB over a 1Gbps Direct Connect takes about seven continuous days.
claims.span_hint: section: Data Gravity and Storage Migration | Stop and think block
claims.anchor_text: At best, that is ~7 days of continuous transfer.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Even before protocol overhead and retries, that transfer takes multiple days of continuous network saturation.
claims.rationale: This is a back-of-envelope calculation presented as an exact fact without a citable source.

claims.claim_text: The module calls rclone the industry standard for S3-to-Ceph RGW migration.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | paragraph 1
claims.anchor_text: Instead, `rclone` is the industry standard.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Instead, tools such as `rclone` can use object-storage APIs directly.
claims.rationale: The rclone capabilities are supportable, but the adoption superlative is not.

claims.claim_text: rclone supports syncing and checking data across cloud/object-storage backends including S3-compatible targets.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | rclone paragraph and commands
claims.rationale: The upstream rclone repository describes rclone as a tool for syncing files with cloud storage and includes S3-compatible backend support.

claims.claim_text: The module calls Velero the undisputed industry standard for Kubernetes state migration.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | Velero paragraph
claims.anchor_text: For comprehensive state migration of native Kubernetes resources (such as CustomResourceDefinitions, Secrets, and ConfigMaps) alongside persistent volumes, **Velero** is the undisputed industry standard tool.
claims.suggested_rewrite: For comprehensive state migration of native Kubernetes resources (such as CustomResourceDefinitions, Secrets, and ConfigMaps) alongside persistent volumes, **Velero** is a Kubernetes backup, restore, and migration tool designed for these workflows.
claims.rationale: Velero's backup and migration role is citable, but the 'undisputed industry standard' superlative is not.

claims.claim_text: Velero backs up, restores, and migrates Kubernetes resources and persistent volumes.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | Velero paragraph
claims.rationale: The upstream Velero repository describes backup, restore, disaster recovery, and Kubernetes cluster resource migration use cases.

claims.claim_text: The module says Velero v1.18.0 was released in March 2025 and introduced concurrent backup processing and cache volume support that drastically reduced RTO.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | Velero paragraph
claims.anchor_text: As of its v1.18.0 release in March 2025, Velero introduced highly anticipated concurrent backup processing and sophisticated cache volume support, drastically reducing recovery time objectives (RTO).
claims.suggested_rewrite: Recent Velero releases added features such as concurrent backup processing and cache-volume configuration for data movement; check upstream release notes for exact version behavior.
claims.rationale: The release date is incorrect and the RTO reduction claim is a performance outcome not established by the release notes.

claims.claim_text: Velero v1.18 release notes include concurrent backup processing and cache volume support.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | Velero paragraph
claims.rationale: The upstream v1.18 release notes list concurrent backup processing and cache-volume/data-movement changes.

claims.claim_text: Broadcom donated Velero to the CNCF Sandbox in 2026.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | Velero paragraph
claims.rationale: The CNCF news item discusses Broadcom donating Velero to CNCF Sandbox.

claims.claim_text: AWS Application Migration Service supports agentless replication from VMware vCenter.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | managed tooling paragraph
claims.rationale: The AWS MGN documentation describes installing the MGN vCenter Client for agentless migration.

claims.claim_text: Classic Azure Migrate retired after February 2024 and classic project inventory metadata was deleted.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | managed tooling paragraph
claims.rationale: Microsoft's Azure Migrate project documentation states that classic Azure Migrate retired in February 2024 and classic metadata would be deleted.

claims.claim_text: The module says Google's Migrate to Containers v1.15.0 was released in May 2024 and deprecated the console UI and migctl.
claims.span_hint: section: S3 to Ceph RGW | managed tooling paragraph
claims.anchor_text: The latter released v1.15.0 in May 2024, notably deprecating the console UI and `migctl` tooling in favor of a strictly local CLI workflow.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Google's Migrate to Containers release notes should be checked for the current CLI workflow and deprecations before choosing that tooling.
claims.rationale: Google's release notes place v1.15.0 in May 2023, so the dated version claim is wrong.

claims.claim_text: Kubernetes API server OIDC flags let the API server trust an OIDC issuer and map username/group claims for RBAC bindings.
claims.span_hint: section: Kubernetes OIDC with Keycloak
claims.rationale: The Kubernetes authentication reference documents OIDC issuer, client ID, username claim, groups claim, and CA options.

claims.claim_text: IRSA uses EKS OIDC, the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation, an admission controller/webhook, and AWS STS credentials for pods.
claims.span_hint: section: Identity and Authentication Translation | IRSA warning
claims.rationale: The EKS IRSA documentation describes the role annotation, OIDC provider, admission controller, and injected AWS credential environment.

claims.claim_text: ExpressRoute is preferred for highest bandwidth and lowest latency private connectivity, while VPN or SD-WAN alternatives are used when ExpressRoute is unavailable.
claims.span_hint: section: Network Connectivity for Migration | paragraph 2
claims.rationale: Microsoft's private connectivity documentation states that ExpressRoute is generally preferred for highest bandwidth and lowest latency.

claims.claim_text: The module says Microsoft explicitly relegates IPsec VPNs to backup/failover because of protocol overhead and internet routing fluctuations.
claims.span_hint: section: Network Connectivity for Migration | paragraph 2
claims.anchor_text: Microsoft's own architectural documentation explicitly ranks ExpressRoute as the preferred networking choice for achieving the absolute highest bandwidth and lowest latency during migration, explicitly relegating traditional IPsec VPNs to a secondary backup or failover role due to their inherent protocol overhead and susceptibility to internet routing fluctuations.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Microsoft documentation generally positions ExpressRoute as the lower-latency, higher-bandwidth private option, with VPN or SD-WAN designs as alternatives or backups when ExpressRoute is unavailable.
claims.rationale: The Microsoft source supports the ExpressRoute preference but not the stronger causal language about protocol overhead and routing fluctuation.

claims.claim_text: The module says Kubernetes v1.35.3 was the latest stable patch released on March 19, 2026.
claims.span_hint: section: Rollback Plan | final paragraph
claims.anchor_text: Ensure your target on-premises infrastructure is actively running a modern, supported standard—such as Kubernetes v1.35.3 (the latest stable patch released on March 19, 2026)—to absolutely guarantee maximum API compatibility with modern cloud-native migration tooling.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Ensure your target on-premises infrastructure is actively running a modern, supported Kubernetes release, and verify the current patch level against the upstream Kubernetes release page before migration.
claims.rationale: Kubernetes v1.36 was released on April 22, 2026, so v1.35.3 is no longer the latest stable Kubernetes release as of this research run.

claims.claim_text: Dropbox moved about 90% of customer data/storage from AWS S3 to Magic Pocket in 2016.
claims.span_hint: section: Did You Know? | item 1
claims.rationale: Dropbox's engineering blog is the primary source for Magic Pocket and the 90% target, but dropbox.tech is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: The module says Dropbox realized about $75M in savings over two years.
claims.span_hint: section: Did You Know? | item 1
claims.anchor_text: realizing estimated savings of ~$75 million over two years
claims.suggested_rewrite: reducing storage operating costs over time
claims.rationale: The exact savings figure needs a primary financial source that is not available in the current allowlist workflow.

claims.claim_text: The module says Dropbox retained unpredictable workloads such as ML training and isolated experiments on AWS.
claims.span_hint: section: Did You Know? | item 1
claims.anchor_text: Crucially, they intelligently retained unpredictable workloads (like ML training models and isolated experiments) on AWS.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Crucially, large migrations can still leave bursty or experimental workloads in public cloud when that operating model fits better.
claims.rationale: The specific workload-retention examples are not supported by the primary Magic Pocket sources found for the storage migration.

claims.claim_text: The module says AWS egress is roughly $0.09/GB, ingress is $0.00/GB, and a 100TB migration costs about $9,200.
claims.span_hint: section: Did You Know? | item 2
claims.anchor_text: AWS charges roughly $0.09/GB to extract your data out of their network, but $0.00/GB to ingest it. Therefore, migrating a 100TB dataset incurs a baseline fee of ~$9,200 just to download the bytes—embodying the classic "Hotel California" pricing model where leaving is intentionally expensive.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Cloud providers commonly charge for outbound data transfer while ingress is often free, so large migrations need an explicit egress-cost estimate before cutover.
claims.rationale: Exact cloud pricing is region-, service-, tier-, and date-dependent, and the simple 100TB calculation ignores tiered pricing.

claims.claim_text: The module says MetalLB BGP failover takes 1 to 3 seconds dictated by the BGP hold timer.
claims.span_hint: section: Did You Know? | item 3
claims.anchor_text: If a designated speaker node suffers a catastrophic hardware failure, another node assumes control in merely 1 to 3 seconds (dictated by the BGP hold timer)—vastly faster than standard DNS failover mechanisms.
claims.suggested_rewrite: If a speaker node fails, route convergence depends on BGP/BFD timers and router configuration rather than DNS TTLs.
claims.rationale: The 1-3 second value is not a default BGP hold-timer fact and depends heavily on BFD/router configuration.

claims.claim_text: The module claims specific Keycloak throughput, Cognito per-user-pool RPS limits, and 500,000 active users for a three-replica Keycloak cluster.
claims.span_hint: section: Did You Know? | item 4
claims.anchor_text: **A self-hosted Keycloak instance routinely handles 2,500+ authentication requests per second** on a single, well-resourced instance. In stark contrast, AWS Cognito enforces a strict soft limit of 120 requests per second per user pool. A properly deployed three-replica Keycloak cluster can smoothly support upwards of 500,000 active users.
claims.suggested_rewrite: **Authentication throughput and quota planning must be benchmarked explicitly.** Keycloak capacity depends on deployment sizing and authentication flow, while managed identity providers publish service quotas that must be checked during migration design.
claims.rationale: The Keycloak and Cognito numbers are benchmark/quota claims that need exact, current primary sources and should not remain as unsupported absolutes.

claims.claim_text: AWS CloudTrail records AWS API activity and can be used to audit AWS API calls.
claims.span_hint: section: Common Mistakes | Forgetting managed service deps row
claims.rationale: The AWS CloudTrail user guide describes CloudTrail as recording AWS API calls and account activity.

claims.claim_text: The Common Mistakes table says to budget $0.09/GB for AWS egress upfront.
claims.span_hint: section: Common Mistakes | Ignoring data egress costs row
claims.anchor_text: | Ignoring data egress costs | Focus on destination | Budget $0.09/GB for AWS egress upfront |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Ignoring data egress costs | Focus on destination | Estimate provider-specific egress charges upfront |
claims.rationale: A fixed AWS egress unit price is too brittle because live prices vary by service, region, destination, and transfer tier.
